title: App Transport Security Bypass - Arbitrary Loads Enabled
description: The application has NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true in its Info.plist App Transport Security configuration, which disables TLS certificate validation for ALL network connections. This allows an attacker on the network to perform man-in-the-middle attacks and intercept all HTTPS traffic in plaintext.
proof_of_concept:
plutil -p Payload/ExampleApp.app/Info.plist | grep -A5 NSAppTransportSecurity

# Output shows:
# NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = true

# To exploit, set up a proxy (Burp Suite, mitmproxy) and intercept all traffic
remediation:
Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true from Info.plist. Instead, use NSExceptionDomains for specific servers that require HTTP or invalid certificates:

```swift
// Info.plist
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <key>NSExceptionDomains</key>
    <dict>
        <key>legacy-server.example.com</key>
        <dict>
            <key>NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads</key>
            <true/>
        </dict>
    </dict>
</dict>
```

title: Keychain Credentials Stored Without Data Protection
description: The application stores sensitive credentials (user session tokens) in the Keychain with kSecAttrAccessibleAlways, which allows access even when the device is locked. This makes credentials accessible to malware or forensic tools.
proof_of_concept:
frida -U -f com.example.app -l keychain-dumper.js --no-pause

# Output shows:
# [+] kSecClassGenericPassword
#     kSecAttrAccount: user@example.com
#     kSecAttrService: com.example.app.session
#     kSecAttrAccessible: kSecAttrAccessibleAlways
#     Data: eyJ0b2tlbiI6ImFiYzEyMzQ1Njc4OSJ9
remediation:
Use kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked or kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly for sensitive data:

```swift
let query: [String: Any] = [
    kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
    kSecAttrAccount as String: account,
    kSecAttrService as String: service,
    kSecAttrAccessible as String: kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly,
    kSecValueData as String: tokenData
]
let status = SecItemAdd(query as CFDictionary, nil)
```

title: URL Scheme Hijacking - Generic Scheme
description: The application registers a generic URL scheme 'myapp://' without host-based validation. Any malicious app can register the same scheme and intercept sensitive data passed via URLs, such as authentication tokens or deep link parameters.
proof_of_concept:
plutil -p Payload/ExampleApp.app/Info.plist | grep -A10 CFBundleURLSchemes

# Create a malicious app with the same scheme:
# 1. Register 'myapp://' in malicious app's Info.plist
# 2. Wait for user to tap a 'myapp://reset-password?token=SECRET' link
# 3. iOS prompts user to choose between apps
# 4. User may select malicious app, leaking the token

# Frida monitoring:
frida -U -f com.example.app -l url-scheme-monitor.js --no-pause

title: Debug Entitlement Enabled in Production Build
description: The application contains get-task-allow=true entitlement in its embedded.mobileprovision, which allows debugger attachment to the running process. This simplifies reverse engineering, dynamic analysis, and runtime manipulation.
proof_of_concept:
codesign -d --entitlements - Payload/ExampleApp.app/ExampleApp

# Output shows:
# <key>get-task-allow</key>
# <true/>

# Attach debugger directly:
debugserver *:1234 -backboard
lldb -n ExampleApp
remediation:
Remove get-task-allow entitlement from release builds. Use Xcode Archive or configure build settings:

```bash
# In Xcode build settings:
Debug Information Format = DWARF with dSYM
Strip Debug Symbols During Copy = Yes

# For manual builds:
codesign --force --sign "iPhone Distribution" --entitlements release.entitlements ExampleApp.app
```

Release entitlements should NOT include:
```xml
<key>get-task-allow</key>
<false/>
```

title: Sensitive Data in NSUserDefaults
description: The application stores session tokens and user preferences in NSUserDefaults without encryption. NSUserDefaults is stored as a plist file in the app's Library/Preferences/ directory and is accessible to anyone with physical device access.
proof_of_concept:
frida -U -f com.example.app -l nsuserdefaults-dumper.js --no-pause

# Output shows:
# [+] NSUserDefaults.standardUserDefaults
#     session_token: eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoxMjM0NX0K
#     last_login: 2024-12-15T10:30:00Z
#     user_preferences: {"notifications": true}

# Manual extraction:
# Device: /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/{GUID}/Library/Preferences/com.example.app.plist
remediation:
Use Keychain for sensitive data (tokens, credentials) instead of NSUserDefaults. For non-sensitive preferences, NSUserDefaults is acceptable:

```swift
// WRONG - storing sensitive data in UserDefaults
UserDefaults.standard.set(authToken, forKey: "session_token")

// CORRECT - use Keychain for sensitive data
let tokenData = authToken.data(using: .utf8)!
let query: [String: Any] = [
    kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
    kSecAttrAccount as String: "session_token",
    kSecAttrService as String: Bundle.main.bundleIdentifier!,
    kSecValueData as String: tokenData,
    kSecAttrAccessible as String: kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked
]
SecItemAdd(query as CFDictionary, nil)
```
